differentiation.extension: Challenge: After writing your one-sentence citation, add one extra sticky note answering this question in one sentence: 'Which interpretation is stronger: that the Revolution is best defined by start/end events, or that it is best defined by the mix of causes and processes? Use two phrases from the excerpt as evidence and explain why they point to your choice.'
differentiation.support: If you get stuck, use this sentence frame: 'The document says the Revolution began with __________ and ended with __________, which shows __________.' One worked example: 'The document says the Revolution began with the Estates General of 1789 and ended with the Coup of 18 Brumaire on 9 November 1799, which shows the author uses these events as start and end dates.' If you need more support, pair a weaker reader with a stronger reader for the debate.

materials: One short printed excerpt of the provided document per pair (teacher prepares a one-paragraph extract that includes the definition sentence and the causes overview)
One sticky note per student
A visible timer or stopwatch (phone or classroom timer)
Whiteboard or chart paper and marker
student_instructions: Read the short document excerpt at your table (one copy per pair). Notice the sentence that defines the French Revolution and the sentences that list causes.
Decide with your partner who will be Speaker A and who will be Speaker B.
Speaker A (1 minute): Argue that the best definition of the French Revolution is the document's phrasing (name the start and end dates exactly as written). Quote the phrase that gives those dates.
Speaker B (1 minute): Argue that the document's definition needs more context about causes (mention at least one long-term and one short-term cause named in the excerpt and explain why that matters).

After both speakers, together write one sentence on a sticky note that cites a phrase from the excerpt to support either the definition (dates) or the causes (choose one). Hand the sticky note to the teacher when asked.
success_criteria: Pairs switch speakers after one minute and both students speak for the allotted time (teacher observes timer and role change).

Each pair's sticky note includes a direct phrase from the excerpt: either the clause naming 'Estates General of 1789' and 'Coup of 18 Brumaire on 9 November 1799' or a short phrase naming 'social, economic, financial and political factors' (teacher inspects notes).
At least three students can quickly point to and read aloud the phrase in the document that gives the start and end dates when asked by the teacher.
teacher_instructions: Before class, print one copy of the document excerpt that contains the exact phrasing of the definition and causes. Arrange students in pairs and give one copy to each pair.

Explain the task to the whole class: say, 'You will hold a two-minute mini-debate inside your pair. One student will argue that the French Revolution should be defined exactly as the document phrases it (start: Estates General 1789; end: Coup of 18 Brumaire, 9 November 1799). The other student will argue that this definition is incomplete or needs context (pointing to multiple causes and elite resistance). Each speaker has 1 minute. Then you will write a 1-sentence citation on a sticky note.'

While pairs debate, circulate and time rounds. Signal when the first minute ends so students switch roles. After both minutes, tell pairs to spend one minute writing a one-sentence citation on the sticky note that uses a phrase from the excerpt to support either claim.

Collect three strong sticky-note citations to read aloud. Ask two quick class-wide follow-up questions (30 seconds each): 'What phrase from the text gives the start and end dates?' and 'Which short-term and long-term causes does the excerpt mention?' Record brief student answers on the board.
activities.title: Two-Minute Claim: When Did the French Revolution Happen?

differentiation.extension: Ask students who finish early to identify one detail in an excerpt that could support a competing interpretation (for example, an excerpt showing popular violence could also be read as evidence of elite fear). Write a short note explaining the two interpretations and which evidence would best decide between them.
differentiation.support: Provide a sentence frame on the evidence sheet: “This excerpt shows (social/economic/political) factor because _____. That helped cause ______, so the Assembly ______.” For groups who need more help, assign a stronger reader as speaker and reduce the task to labeling only two excerpts and writing one sentence about one of them.

materials: One copy per group of a short evidence sheet (teacher prints 1 page with three short excerpts: Estates‑General call, eyewitness line about Bastille, text of an August Decree clause) — teacher can prepare in 10 minutes
Timer or stopwatch
One sheet of scrap paper and a pen per group
student_instructions: 1. In your group of three, read the three short excerpts on the evidence sheet together.

2. For each excerpt, decide which kind of factor it best shows: social (religion, class, privileges), economic (taxes, debt, food prices), or political (representation, royal power, law). Write the factor word next to that excerpt on your scrap paper.
3. Choose one excerpt and write one clear sentence that explains how that excerpt helped move events from the Estates‑General toward the August Decrees (use facts from the excerpt).
4. Pick one person to speak for 30 seconds to tell the class your chosen excerpt and your one-sentence explanation.
success_criteria: Each group labels all three excerpts with one of the categories: social, economic, or political.
Each group writes a one-sentence explanation that links a specific detail from an excerpt to a step between the Estates‑General and the August Decrees.
Two groups deliver a 30‑second summary that mentions the excerpt and the claimed causal link (e.g., ‘Because X in this excerpt shows Y, the National Assembly responded by Z’).
teacher_instructions: 1. Arrange students in groups of 3. Hand each group the evidence sheet, one scrap paper, and tell them they have 8 minutes for the task. Start the timer and say: “You will read three short excerpts about 1789. Decide together: which social, economic or political factor does each excerpt best show? Then pick one excerpt and explain how it helped move France from Estates‑General to the August Decrees.”

2. While groups work, circulate. Pause any group after 4 minutes and ask one probing question aloud to the class (rotate each round): “Which factor —social, economic, or political— is strongest in that excerpt?” Do not give answers; only prompt groups that are stuck to use the sentence frames on the support slip.
3. With 1 minute remaining, tell groups to choose one speaker to give a 30‑second summary to the class. When time is up, call two groups to each give their 30‑second summary (total 1 minute).

4. After the two summaries, ask a final 30‑second whole-class question: “Which excerpt could be interpreted more than one way? Give a one-sentence reason.” Collect one scrap paper from each group as their evidence-based claim.
activities.title: Three Moments, One Crisis: Small-Group Evidence Discussion

differentiation.extension: After performing, write a one-paragraph note as your role advising a member of the National Convention (fall 1792). Use at least two pieces of evidence from the slips to recommend a specific policy (for example, how to handle church property or how to treat the former king) and explain how your recommendation anticipates political consequences.
differentiation.support: Pair a student who struggles with a stronger reader; give the struggling student this sentence frame to use in the speech: 'On [date/event] the Assembly did X (evidence). Because of that, my group believes Y. We also understand that others say Z, but we respond...'. If time is tight, reduce the performance to 60 seconds (45s statement, 15s rebuttal).

materials: 3 index cards labeled 'Constitutional Clergy (oath supporters)'
3 index cards labeled 'Non-juring Clergy (refusers)'
3 index cards labeled 'Active Citizens / National Guards'
3 index cards labeled 'Royalists / King’s Household'
1 clock or stopwatch
1 printed short evidence slip per role (teacher prepares 1 paragraph each, see teacher step 2)
chalkboard or whiteboard and marker
student_instructions: You are in a 3–4 person group assigned one historical role: Constitutional Clergy (support oath), Non-juring Clergy (refuse oath), Active Citizens/National Guard, or Royalists/King’s Household.

Read the evidence slip your teacher gives you. Your group must: (1) include that factual sentence exactly once in your spoken lines as evidence, (2) state your position about the clergy oath and the king’s actions, and (3) include one short line acknowledging why another role might reasonably disagree.

Plan a 90-second main speech that uses the evidence slip to support your view, and prepare a 30-second rebuttal reacting to an imagined opposing point (your teacher will time you). Speak in role; give reasons that link social, economic, and political factors: mention confiscation/assignats or the Civil Constitution (12 July 1790), the Flight to Varennes (June 1791), or the Insurrection of 10 August 1792 where appropriate.

Perform when your group is called: one person speaks the main statement, others add the rebuttal. Use clear evidence language like 'On 12 July 1790 the Assembly...' or 'After the Flight to Varennes in June 1791...' and end with a one-sentence claim about whether the monarchy can be trusted.
success_criteria: Each performing group says the factual sentence from their evidence slip aloud during their 90-second statement.

Observers hear at least one explicit connection in each performance between a specific event (Civil Constitution 12 July 1790, confiscation/assignats, Flight to Varennes June 1791, or Insurrection 10 August 1792) and the group’s position.
In each group’s rebuttal a student acknowledges at least one plausible opposing interpretation (for example, a Constitutional Cleric names why Non-juring Clergy fear state control).
teacher_instructions: 1. Arrange students into 12 small groups of 3–4. Tell them each group will role-play one of four perspectives: Constitutional Clergy, Non-juring Clergy, Active Citizens/National Guard, or Royalists. Distribute the labeled index cards so each role is covered by at least three groups. Say: “You have 12 minutes to prepare and perform a 2-minute role-play showing your group’s response to the requirement that clergy swear the Civil Constitution of the Clergy and how the king’s flight and recent defeats affect your trust in the monarchy.”

2. Hand each group a printed evidence slip (one paragraph) tailored to their role. Each slip must contain one factual sentence from the period (e.g., date of the Civil Constitution of the Clergy: 12 July 1790; that church property was confiscated to back assignats; that Louis XVI attempted to flee in June 1791; that 10 August 1792 was an insurrection leading to the monarchy’s fall). Instruct groups to use that sentence as a piece of evidence in their role-play and to include one opposing interpretation (a brief line suggesting why another group might disagree).

3. Give groups 6 minutes to plan: one student will speak for 90 seconds in the performance, others will add a 30-second rebuttal line. While they plan, circulate and check each group’s evidence slip is used in a complete sentence and that they include one specific reference to either confiscation of church property/assignats, the Civil Constitution (12 July 1790), the Flight to Varennes (June 1791), or the Insurrection of 10 August 1792. Prompt with questions if a group stalls (e.g., “How does the king’s flight change your trust?”).

4. Run performances: call groups in role order so contrasting perspectives are adjacent (for example: Constitutional Clergy, Non-juring Clergy, Active Citizens, Royalists, then repeat). Time each performance: 2 minutes per group (90-second statement + 30-second rebuttal). After each group, ask one quick clarifying question aloud (e.g., “Which specific action from 1791 or 1792 most influenced your position?”) and move on.

5. Close with a 90-second whole-class wrap: write three headlines on the board from students’ plays that show (a) how confiscation and the Civil Constitution divided opinion, (b) how the Flight to Varennes damaged the monarchy’s credibility, and (c) how these divisions helped lead to the Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and the Republic. Collect the evidence slips.
activities.title: Debate at the Tuileries: Who Should Swear the Oath?

differentiation.extension: Choose one station and write a two-paragraph mini-essay on the chart: first paragraph outlines how the specific event (e.g., Committee of Public Safety) can be seen as a response to immediate threats; second paragraph presents a competing historical interpretation that emphasizes longer-term structural causes (social/economic) and cites at least one piece of evidence from another station to support that interpretation.
differentiation.support: Pair students heterogeneously so one stronger reader works with one who needs support. If a pair cannot start, use this sentence frame to begin their chart: "This source says _____ (copy 3–6 words). This suggests that _____ because _____." As a worked first item, at Station 1 write: "Source: '22 September 1792... Year One.' This suggests the Convention wanted a complete break from monarchy because they reset the calendar to Year One. Alternatively: some representatives may have chosen a new calendar to mark legal changes, not only to erase the past."

materials: 4 printed source slips (one per station) — teacher-prepared from textbook or handouts
chart paper or large sticky notes for each station
markers (one per pair)
timer or stopwatch
taped signs to mark 4 stations around the room
student_instructions: You are in a pair. You will visit four stations for this 12-minute gallery walk. At each station you will have 2.5 minutes.

At each station do these three things on the chart paper: (1) Copy one clear factual piece of evidence from the printed source slip (one sentence). (2) Write a one-sentence interpretation that explains how that evidence connects to the station’s concept (Republic proclamation; Louis’s trial/execution; Committee of Public Safety; or causes of the Estates General). Use the phrase “This suggests…” to start your sentence. (3) Write a one-sentence alternative interpretation or a question that challenges your interpretation, starting with “Alternatively…” or “What if…?”.
Rotate when your teacher or the timer signals. Keep your writing large and legible so others can read it. Do not erase others’ notes; instead add your own line if a chart already has writing.
Be ready at the end to share one chart line from a station you visited. Base your sharing on text evidence — say which word or sentence on the source slip supports your interpretation.
success_criteria: At least three stations show one clear factual sentence copied from the printed source slip (teacher can read it while circulating).
Most pairs have written an interpretation that begins with “This suggests…” and links the evidence to the stated concept for that station.
At least two stations include an alternative interpretation or question that starts with “Alternatively…” or “What if…?”
teacher_instructions: Before class: prepare four stations placed around the room. At each station place a printed source slip (see guidance below) and a blank sheet of chart paper with the station number. Station 1: Proclamation of the First Republic (22 Sept 1792). Station 2: Trial and execution of Louis XVI (Jan 1793). Station 3: Creation and role of the Committee of Public Safety (6 Apr 1793). Station 4: Evidence connecting social/economic/political crisis to calling the Estates General (1789).

Arrange students into pairs and tell them the activity lasts 12 minutes. Explain that pairs will rotate through all four stations spending 2.5 minutes at each station, plus 1 minute at the start for directions and 0.5 minutes buffer. Start the timer and announce rotations aloud.

When a pair arrives at a station they read the printed source slip and then: (a) write one sentence of factual evidence from the slip on the chart paper, (b) write one short interpretation that connects that evidence to one of the three target concepts (Republic proclamation, Louis's trial/execution, Committee of Public Safety) or to causes leading to the Estates General, and (c) add a one-sentence alternative interpretation or question that challenges the first interpretation. Circulate and prompt pairs who are stuck with one targeted question from the support scaffolds.

After 12 minutes, call students back to their seats. Spend 4 minutes whole-class: ask 3 different pairs to read one chart entry aloud (one factual evidence, one interpretation, one alternative interpretation). Conclude by reminding students how competing interpretations and evidence link to the objective about causes of 1789; assign follow-up reading as needed.
activities.title: Gallery Walk: From Republic Proclamation to Louis's Execution

differentiation.extension: Choose one pair of adjacent events on the final wall and prepare a two-minute oral argument presenting a competing interpretation: explain one historian's view that emphasizes political causes and another that emphasizes social or economic causes. Cite at least two different pieces of evidence from the packet to support each interpretation.
differentiation.support: Pair students so one is stronger in reading. Provide this sentence frame to start link-sentences: 'Because [specific fact or date], this led to [next event] by increasing/decreasing [social/economic/political pressure].' Example worked first item: Slip A: 'Sept 1793–July 1794: Reign of Terror — ~300,000 arrests, ~16,600 executed.' Slip B: 'July 1794: Thermidorian Reaction ends the Terror.' Example link sentence: 'Because about 16,600 people were executed during the Terror, widespread fear and backlash grew and led to the Thermidorian Reaction.'

materials: Printed timeline slips (one event per slip) — teacher prepares 10 slips listing short dated statements from 1793–1799 (see teacher list below)
Tape or sticky tack
Stopwatch or classroom clock
Clipboard or notebook and pen for each student pair
Textbook or printed packet with the activity's three concept summaries (one per pair)
student_instructions: Work with your partner. You will get a stack of event slips. Read your textbook packet before placing slips.

Place the slips on the wall in the order you think they happened from earliest (left) to latest (right). For each pair of neighbouring slips, write one short sentence on your clipboard that explains why those two events are linked. Use a specific fact or number from the packet (for example, 'about 16,600 executions') as evidence.
If you disagree about order, each partner must state one piece of evidence for their view; then decide and write the evidence you used.
When time is called, write one sentence answering: 'Which factor (social, economic, or political) mattered most in moving from the Reign of Terror to the Directory? Give one piece of evidence.'
success_criteria: Pairs have the slips arranged left-to-right showing a plausible chronological sequence (e.g., Reign of Terror items left of Thermidorian items, Directory items left of 18 Brumaire items).
Each pair has written at least three link-sentences that each include a specific piece of evidence from the packet (a date, institution name, or statistic).
Each pair completed the one-sentence exit answer citing a factor and a specific supporting fact.
teacher_instructions: Before class, cut up and prepare 10 timeline slips (examples below) and make one set per 4–5 pairs. Put pairs into groups of two students. Tell students they will place events in order on the classroom wall and add one sentence of evidence-based interpretation to explain causal links.

Start the activity with this prompt aloud: 'You have 12 minutes to place these events from the Reign of Terror through 18 Brumaire in chronological order on the wall and write one short evidence-based reason that links each adjacent event. Use the textbook packet for facts and statistics.' Give each pair one slip at a time from the set. Start the timer for 12 minutes.

While students work, circulate. For each pair, check that they cite at least one piece of evidence from the packet (a number, date, or named institution) and ask one clarifying question: 'What evidence are you using to connect these two events?' If a pair is stuck after 3 minutes, offer the support sentence frame on the support sheet.

With 2 minutes remaining, call 'Freeze.' Ask one volunteer pair to read one link aloud. Collect a quick whole-class exit note: each pair writes a one-sentence answer to 'Which single factor (social, economic, or political) do you think mattered most in moving from the Terror to the Directory? Give one piece of evidence.'
activities.title: Timeline Walk: Tracing the Terror to 18 Brumaire

differentiation.extension: Ask: ‘Compare the end of the Terror to the establishment of the Directory: which change was deeper — the end of the Terror (immediate political purges) or the new Constitution of Year III (longer-term institutional change)? Use at least two pieces of evidence: one about Thermidorian actions and one about the Constitution’s property-based indirect elections. Be prepared to explain which change mattered more for ordinary citizens’ daily lives.'
differentiation.support: If you cannot start, use this sentence frame and the worked example. Sentence frame: ‘I claim that __________ because the evidence shows __________ (date or law). For example, Robespierre’s execution on 28 July caused the Convention to act because they feared his power and then repealed the Law of 22 Prairial.’ Worked first item: take the slip about Robespierre’s arrest and read: ‘Robespierre was arrested after a denunciation, attempted suicide, and executed on 28 July. This shows the Convention turned against him, which helps explain why they then repealed the Law of 22 Prairial.’ Pair a lower-starting student with a stronger speaker as evidence reader.

materials: Printed short evidence slips (one per group) — 4 slips total, each with a short quote or fact (see teacher instructions for content)
Stopwatch or visible timer
Whiteboard or chart paper and marker
Seats arranged for two debating sides
student_instructions: You are debating the motion: “The fall of Robespierre was the primary cause of the end of the Terror.”
Step 1 — Choose your stance: Your teacher has assigned your team as either affirmative (Agree) or negative (Disagree).
Step 2 — Pick an evidence slip: One team member goes to a station and chooses one of the four evidence slips. Read it aloud to your team and decide how it supports your side.

Step 3 — Prepare your case (6 minutes): Use the slip and your knowledge to make two linked points: a claim (your reason) and one piece of evidence from the slip or from class facts (for example: Robespierre’s execution on 28 July; the Law of 22 Prairial denied defence; repeal of Prairial; Constitution of Year III created the Directory). The evidence reader reads the slip in the debate.

Step 4 — Debate format and timing: Each speaker gets 60 seconds to speak. Affirmative speaker 1 opens, negative speaker 1 responds, affirmative speaker 2 rebuts, negative speaker 2 rebuts, then 60 seconds for each team’s final summary. Use your remaining team members to hold up one short evidence phrase on a card when it’s referenced (e.g., “Prairial denied defence”).

Step 5 — Focus on evidence and competing interpretations: During your remarks cite the slip or a fact and explain whether it shows causation (Robespierre’s fall led directly to change) or shows other causes (laws, institutions, ongoing violence).
success_criteria: Each team cites at least one explicit fact from a slip aloud (e.g., ‘Robespierre executed on 28 July’ or ‘Law of 22 Prairial denied defence’).
Each team speaker responds to an opponent’s point with a specific counter-evidence or interpretation (e.g., points to repeal of Prairial or to Constitution of Year III).

Note-takers produce one clear concluding sentence on chart paper that links a cause to a consequence (for example: ‘Robespierre’s execution allowed the Convention to repeal Prairial and close the Jacobin Club’).
teacher_instructions: 1. Before class (2 minutes): Prepare four short evidence slips on plain paper: A) description of Robespierre's arrest, suicide attempt and execution on 28 July; B) text summary of the Law of 22 Prairial (10 June) and its denial of defence leading to more executions; C) notes on Thermidorian revenge actions, closing of Jacobin Club and repeal of Prairial; D) summary of the Constitution of Year III and Directory institutions. Place one slip at each of four group stations.

2. Grouping and roles (1 minute): Divide the class into two debate teams (affirmative and negative), each with 4–6 students. Within each team assign: two speakers, one evidence reader, one note-taker, and remaining students as rebuttal/supporters.

3. Launch (1 minute): Tell students: “You will debate the motion: ‘The fall of Robespierre was the primary cause of the end of the Terror.’ The affirmative argues yes; the negative argues no (emphasizing laws, institutions, or other factors). Each team will pick one evidence slip from the four stations (teams may choose different slips). Start the 12-minute timer now.”

4. While students work (12 minutes): Monitor time with the visible timer. At 8 minutes announce: “Two minutes to prepare final rebuttal.” Circulate, read each team’s notes, and quietly prompt students who are stuck by asking: “Which concrete fact from your slip supports your claim?” Do not offer answers, only questions to push evidence linking.

5. Closing (1 minute after debate): Have each team’s note-taker read one sentence that states the team’s strongest evidence-based reason. Collect note-taker sheets or photos of the chart paper for assessment.
activities.title: Thermidor Debate: Who Caused the End of the Terror?

differentiation.extension: For early finishers: write a 3–4 sentence paragraph on your scrap paper that compares the evidence you read about the Terror with one fact about the Directory (from class notes). Does the evidence suggest the Directory continued the same problems (military reliance, corruption) or reacted against them? Use at least one phrase from your slip as a citation and name one opposing interpretation.
differentiation.support: If you are unsure how to start, use this sentence frame: “This excerpt suggests that [short cause or event] contributed to the Terror because it shows [brief evidence].” Example (worked): “This excerpt suggests that mass mobilisation increased fear because it describes conscription and large armies moving across borders.” Pair a weaker reader with a stronger reader and ask the stronger reader to read aloud first.

materials: One printed evidence slip per group (4 short primary/secondary excerpts; teacher can cut and hand out)
A timer or stopwatch (phone is fine)
One sheet of scrap paper or a sticky note per group
Whiteboard or chart paper and marker
student_instructions: 1. In your group of 3, read the printed slip aloud once together. The slip is a short primary or secondary excerpt connected to 1793–94.

2. Decide as a group whether the excerpt best shows: a cause of the Reign of Terror, a direct consequence of it, or evidence explaining why Thermidor (the backlash) happened. Mark your choice on your sticky note.
3. Write one clear claim (short sentence) on the sticky note that uses the excerpt as evidence. Under the claim, copy one phrase or sentence from the slip as your citation.

4. At the 7-minute signal, pass your slip to the next group, read that new slip quickly, and add one sentence on your sticky note that links the new slip to your original claim or to a different heading (cause / consequence / Thermidor).
5. At the end, place your sticky note under Causes, Consequences, or Reasons for Thermidor on the board. Be ready to read your one-sentence claim aloud if called on.
success_criteria: Each group has placed a sticky note labeled Cause, Consequence, or Reason for Thermidor on the board.
While circulating, teacher hears at least one student in each group read a direct phrase or sentence from their slip to support their claim.

At least two groups offer different interpretations aloud (for example: one frames the Terror as defensive mobilisation, another as factional power struggle) when the teacher restates competing interpretations.
teacher_instructions: 1. Before class (or in the first minute): divide students into groups of 3. Hand each group a single printed evidence slip. Say: “You have 14 minutes to read your slip, discuss how it helps explain either (A) a cause of the Reign of Terror, (B) a consequence of it, or (C) why Thermidor followed, and be ready to share one claim and one piece of evidence.” Start the timer for 14 minutes.

2. While groups work (minutes 0–9): circulate. For each group check they have read the slip aloud once, and ask one probing question: “Which specific action, event, or social pressure in this excerpt points to a cause or consequence?” Do not lecture; listen for students using the text to support claims.

3. Midway (at 7 minutes): announce a 60-second mini-rotate. Each group passes their slip to the next group and reads the new slip quickly, then adds one new note on their sticky note connecting the new slip to either the Terror or Thermidor. Restart the timer for the remaining 7 minutes.
4. Final minute: call time. Ask each group to pin or place their sticky note on the board under one of three headings you write on the board beforehand: Causes | Consequences | Reasons for Thermidor.

5. Wrap-up (final 2 minutes of the 14): pick three groups (a group that received different slips) to read their sticky note aloud. After each read, briefly (30 seconds) state aloud two competing interpretations you heard while circulating (for example: was the Terror a necessary defensive measure, or primarily a result of political factionalism?). End by giving a one-sentence class summary linking violence, mobilisation, and political reaction.
activities.title: Four-Source Round: Causes and Consequences of the Terror

differentiation.extension: Ask the group to add a 30-second epilogue in which a character predicts how the symbols or assignats will be remembered by future historians; require citation of one additional primary-type detail from the chapter (for example, the 1795 adoption of La Marseillaise or the 1796 withdrawal of assignats) and explain how historians might disagree about its importance.
differentiation.support: Pair a stronger reader with a student who needs help and reduce roles to three (combine Moderate Citizen and Newspaper Editor). Use this sentence frame for each speech: "As [role], I believe ___ because the chapter says __ (date or short quote)." Example first line for the Newspaper Editor: "As the Editor, I printed La Marseillaise in 1792 because Rouget de Lisle composed it that year and the chapter shows it became a revolutionary song."

materials: Printed role slips (one per student) — teacher prepares in 5–10 minutes
One copy of the chapter or textbook passage for each group (or projected key excerpts)
Timer or stopwatch (phone or classroom clock)
One sheet of chart paper and a marker per group
student_instructions: You are in a group of four. Each of you has a role: Revolutionary Supporter, Moderate Citizen, Woman Activist, and Newspaper Editor (role slips name one).

Step 1 (2 minutes): Read your role slip and the small excerpt of the chapter your group has. Decide who will speak first. Plan a 5-minute role play in which each person speaks as their character and uses at least one piece of evidence from the chapter (a date, a short quote, or a fact). Your play must include at least two of these topics: La Marseillaise, a revolutionary symbol (cockade/tricolore/liberty cap), the guillotine, women's political role, or assignats/price controls.

Step 2 (5 minutes): Perform your role play for the class. In the performance, each character must: state one piece of chapter evidence aloud, offer a perspective on a symbol or economic issue, and respond to another character with a competing interpretation.

Step 3 (3 minutes): After the performance, work together to write on chart paper: (a) two ways newspapers or symbols influenced public perception during the Revolution, each with the chapter evidence you used, and (b) one competing interpretation you presented in the play.
Be ready to present your group's chart paper in 1 minute.
success_criteria: Each group performs a role play in which all four students speak and at least two different Revolution topics from the chapter are mentioned aloud.
During performances, students state specific chapter evidence (a date, short quote, or named fact) at least twice per group.
Each group's chart paper lists two concrete ways newspapers or symbols influenced public perception and cites the chapter evidence used in the play.
teacher_instructions: 1. Arrange students in groups of four. Give each student a role slip (see roles below) and give each group a copy of the chapter excerpts or project the same excerpts for all to see. Explain: 'You will do a 7-minute role play and a 5-minute reporting/reflection.' Start the timer at the beginning of the role-play phase.

2. Read aloud to the whole class: "Use evidence from the chapter to make your character speak about at least two symbolic or economic issues from the Revolution (La Marseillaise, cockade/tricolore/liberty cap, guillotine, women's political role, or assignats/price controls). Present competing perspectives—why different people saw the same symbol differently." Then instruct groups to plan for 2 minutes and perform for 5 minutes.

3. While groups plan and perform, circulate quickly: listen for specific chapter evidence (dates, quotes, or facts) and remind groups to state the evidence aloud in the play if they forget (e.g., 'Rouget de Lisle wrote La Marseillaise in 1792'). Note one example from 2–3 groups to share later.

4. After performances, give each group 3 minutes to write on chart paper: (a) two ways newspapers or symbols influenced public perception (each must cite chapter evidence), and (b) one example of a competing interpretation they used. Then call two groups to present their chart paper (1 minute each).

5. Conclude with a 1-minute whole-class prompt: ask students to vote by show of hands whether a given symbol (teacher names one) was mainly unifying or mainly divisive, and ask one student to state the chapter evidence behind the vote.
activities.title: Symbols and Voices: A 12-Minute Role Play on Revolutionary Symbols and Economics

differentiation.extension: Choose one station and write a 4–6 sentence mini-argument on the back of the chart paper: use two different sources from the station area (e.g., a newspaper quote and a bibliographic note about assignats or the guillotine) to argue which had the stronger long-term impact on public perception in France — newspapers or symbols — and explain how that influence later affected another European country (cite a bibliography entry).
differentiation.support: Pair a struggling student with a confident partner. Provide this sentence frame to start: “The text says ‘______’ (cite page). items.answer: Socially, France was deeply divided: the privileged First and Second Estates enjoyed legal exemptions while the Third Estate (peasants, urban workers and bourgeoisie) bore heavy taxes and resented inequalities — this widespread popular discontent created pressure for change. Economically, repeated poor harvests, rising bread prices and a heavy national debt (exacerbated by war spending) produced hardship and a fiscal crisis; the government could not raise enough revenue without reform. Politically, the ruling elite resisted meaningful reform and the king’s ministers were indecisive, so attempts to solve the fiscal emergency failed. Together these factors produced a fiscal and political deadlock: unable to implement reforms alone and facing unrest, Louis XVI called the Estates‑General in May 1789 to seek consent for taxation and break the impasse. The Third Estate’s later breakaway into a National Assembly in June shows how the social grievances and political stalemate escalated after the Estates‑General convened.

1) Newspapers and pamphlets spread revolutionary ideas and shaped popular opinion by reporting events, arguing political positions, and encouraging participation. Evidence: the chapter notes that over 130 newspapers appeared in 1789 and more than 2,000 were founded in the following decade; these publications debated issues, publicised grievances, and mobilised support for actions such as petitions and protests. By increasing the flow of information and opinion, newspapers turned private complaints into public causes and made political debate part of everyday life.

2) Revolutionary symbols — for example the cockade, the tricolore and La Marseillaise — created shared identity and emotional commitment to the Revolution, signalling who belonged to the new political community. Evidence: the chapter describes the blue-and-red cockade of Paris and the Phrygian liberty cap as widely used emblems linking the movement to republican and classical traditions, and records that La Marseillaise was composed in 1792 and adopted by the National Convention as the anthem in 1795. These symbols simplified complex ideas into visible signs and songs that could be recognised, worn or sung in public, strengthening solidarity and marking people as supporters of revolutionary change.

items.answer: The Storming of the Bastille (14 July 1789) was important because it became a powerful symbol of popular opposition to royal authority and forced the revolutionary government to respond. Two specific effects were: (1) it helped to legitimise and strengthen Parisian revolutionary forces — for example, the formation and recognition of the Parisian National Guard and the elevation of popular leaders, which shifted power toward popular revolutionary organisations; (2) it accelerated political change by pressuring the National Assembly to adopt radical measures shortly afterwards, such as the August Decrees that began to abolish feudal privileges and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, showing the Assembly responding to popular demands. Together these effects show how the Bastille triggered both immediate popular mobilisation and a series of radical acts by the Assembly.

levels.descriptor: Clearly explains the significance and gives two specific, accurate effects linked to Assembly actions or revolutionary change (e.g., recognition/strengthening of revolutionary forces such as the National Guard; pressure leading to the August Decrees and the Declaration of the Rights of Man).

items.answer: The Assembly confiscated church property to solve the fiscal crisis: nationalising church lands provided assets that could be used to back new paper money (assignats) and to pay state debts. On 12 July 1790 the Civil Constitution of the Clergy made the Catholic clergy employees of the state, reorganised dioceses to match new départements, required election of priests and bishops, and compelled clergy to swear an oath of loyalty to the constitution. Politically and socially, these measures stabilised government finance in the short term by creating assignats backed by national lands, but they deeply divided the church and French society. The required oath split priests into ‘jurors’ (those who swore) and ‘non-jurors’ or refractory clergy (those who refused), alienating many devout peasants and provoking resistance in the countryside. This religious rupture fuelled counter-revolutionary activity, weakened moderate support for the Revolution, and intensified polarisation between revolutionaries and traditionalists. Historians debate the interpretation: some argue the reforms were necessary to secularise and rationalise France and to secure finance; others see them as politically reckless, needlessly antagonising popular religion and helping to produce internal conflict.

The rule of 'active citizens' limited participation by allowing only adult men who met property or tax qualifications (and sometimes age or residency requirements) to vote and hold office, excluding women, the poor, and many urban workers from political rights.

items.answer: By summer 1792 a series of military setbacks (notably defeats at Verdun and the Brunswick Manifesto which threatened Paris) increased fear that the revolutionary government and the nation were endangered. These defeats undermined confidence in King Louis XVI, who was suspected of royalist sympathy and collusion with foreign powers. At the same time Paris saw growing popular insurrection: armed fédérés and sans-culottes, radical deputies (like the Commune of Paris) and revolutionary newspapers pushed for direct action. On 10 August 1792 insurgents and National Guard elements attacked the Tuileries Palace, where the king sheltered with his Swiss Guards. The fighting led to the massacre or disarmament of the Swiss Guards, the suspension and arrest of the king, and the effective end of royal authority. The Legislative Assembly then called elections for a National Convention which abolished the monarchy and, in September 1792, proclaimed the French First Republic. Historians disagree about causes: one interpretation emphasizes structural pressures — military defeats and foreign threats making the king politically untenable — while another stresses social and political radicalisation in Paris (economic hardship, popular politics, and republican agitation) as the decisive force. Both factors together best explain why the monarchy fell on 10 August and why republicans moved quickly to found the Republic in September.

items.answer: The Committee of Public Safety, created on 6 April 1793, became the Convention’s central executive body during a period of internal crisis and external war. It came to dominate the Convention because the Convention delegated emergency powers to it to coordinate war effort and internal security, and because leading revolutionaries (for example, Robespierre and Saint-Just) used their influence within the Committee to push policy. Two main powers or actions it exercised were: (1) directing the military and organizing levées en masse and centralised war administration to defend France against foreign armies; and (2) supervising the policing and judicial machinery at home, for example by creating representatives on mission and supporting the Revolutionary Tribunal to arrest, try and execute suspected counter‑revolutionaries. Historians link the Committee to the Reign of Terror because its emergency powers and authority over policing and tribunals made repression systematic: its belief that revolutionary survival justified harsh measures, combined with urgent wartime pressures and weak legal safeguards, led to widespread use of summary trials and executions. Some historians emphasise intentional policy from Committee leaders; others argue the Terror resulted more from situation and institutional incentives (war, economic crisis, and delegated powers) than a single conspiratorial plan.
